summary: Describes the MD2 message-digest algorithm, which takes input of any length and produces a 128-bit fingerprint, or message digest. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 6149, which retires it.

plainLanguage.summary: MD2 is a message-digest algorithm: it takes a message of any length and produces a 128-bit fingerprint, short enough to sign with a private key. RFC 1319 describes the algorithm in five steps, gives a reference implementation in C, and lists test results to check an implementation against. The RFC is now Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 6149.

subtitle: The 1992 hash function that turns any message into a 128-bit fingerprint.

tldr.problem: Digital signature schemes need a way to compress a large message, of any length, into a short fixed-size value that changes completely when the message changes, so a private key can sign the short value instead of the whole message.
tldr.mechanism: MD2 pads the message to a multiple of 16 bytes, appends a 16-byte checksum built from a permutation table derived from the digits of pi, then runs each 16-byte block through 18 rounds of byte substitution and mixing in a 48-byte buffer, outputting the first 16 bytes as the digest.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 6149; its own text calls the design new in 1992 and says further security analysis was justified.

facts.label: Permutation table
facts.value: 256 bytes, from the digits of pi

today: RFC 1319 is an Informational RFC from April 1992 that is now Historic, and RFC 6149 obsoletes it.

sections.title: What MD2 Is For
sections.content:
MD2 is a message-digest algorithm: it takes a message of arbitrary length and produces a 128-bit fingerprint, also called a message digest. The RFC states the design goal in the usual terms for such functions: it is conjectured to be computationally infeasible either to produce two messages with the same digest, or to produce any message that has a given, prechosen digest.

The intended use is digital signature applications. There a large file must be compressed in a secure manner before it is signed with a private key under a public-key cryptosystem such as RSA. License to use MD2 is granted for non-commercial Internet Privacy-Enhanced Mail.

RFC 1319 updates the August 1989 RFC 1115, which also contained a reference implementation. The main differences are that RFC 1319 adds a textual description of the algorithm and a more portable reference implementation. For OSI-based applications the RFC gives the algorithm's object identifier, md2 OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= {iso(1) member-body(2) US(840) rsadsi(113549) digestAlgorithm(2) 2}, and says that in the X.509 AlgorithmIdentifier the parameters for MD2 should have type NULL.
sections.plainLanguage: MD2 compresses any message into a 128-bit fingerprint that can be signed with a private key. The document defines the algorithm, its identifier for directory systems, and a portable reference implementation.

sections.title: The Five Steps of MD2
sections.content:
Take a message of b bytes, written as m_0 m_1 ... m_{b-1}, where b may be zero or arbitrarily large. Computing its digest takes five steps.

Step 1, append padding bytes. Extend the message so its length in bytes is a multiple of 16. Padding is always performed, even when the length already divides by 16: append i bytes of value i until the length is right, so at least one byte and at most 16 bytes are added. Call the result M[0 ... N-1], with N a multiple of 16.

Step 2, append checksum. Compute a 16-byte checksum C of the message and append it. The checksum uses a 256-byte permutation table S, constructed from the digits of pi, as a non-linear byte substitution. Starting with the checksum cleared and a carry byte L set to zero, each byte c of the message in turn is replaced by S[c xor L], and the new value becomes the next L, chaining through all 16 bytes of each block in order. The checksum is appended, giving a new length N' = N + 16.

Step 3, initialize the MD buffer. A 48-byte buffer X holds the running state and is initialized to zero.

Step 4, process the message in 16-byte blocks. For each block, copy it into X[16 ... 31], and fill X[32 ... 47] with the block exclusive-ored with the current state X[0 ... 15]. Then do 18 rounds. In each round every byte of the 48-byte buffer is exclusive-ored in turn with S entries selected by a running table index t, and after each round t advances by the round number, taken modulo 256.

Step 5, output. The message digest is the first 16 bytes of the buffer, X[0 ... 15].

The RFC's summary puts the security on numbers: the difficulty of finding two messages with the same digest is conjectured to be on the order of 2^64 operations, and the difficulty of finding any message with a given digest on the order of 2^128 operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is padded to a multiple of 16 bytes, then given a 16-byte checksum made from a table of numbers taken from the digits of pi. A 48-byte work area mixes each 16-byte block in 18 rounds, and its first 16 bytes are the fingerprint.

sections.title: Reference Implementation and Test Suite
sections.content:
The appendix reproduces a reference implementation in C, taken from RSAREF, a cryptographic toolkit for Privacy-Enhanced Mail: a header file defining the MD2 context, with a 16-byte state, a 16-byte checksum, a byte count modulo 16 and a 16-byte input buffer, and the MD2 source itself with MD2Init, MD2Update and MD2Final as the entry points.

A test driver accompanies the implementation. It digests strings, times a run over 1000 blocks of 1000 bytes, digests a file or standard input, and can run a fixed test suite. The RFC prints the expected results of that suite, so any implementation can be checked against them, for example MD2("") = 8350e5a3e24c153df2275c9f80692773 and MD2("abc") = da853b0d3f88d99b30283a69e6ded6bb. The driver compiles for MD5 by default and for MD2 or MD4 when the MD symbol is set on the compiler command line.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC ships working C code and a list of known-good outputs for sample inputs, so a new implementation can prove it behaves the same way.

sections.title: Security Claim and Current Status
sections.content:
The RFC's own security assessment is brief: the level of security discussed is considered sufficient for implementing very high security hybrid digital signature schemes based on MD2 and a public-key cryptosystem. It also notes in the summary that MD2 had been carefully scrutinized for weaknesses, but was a relatively new algorithm, so further security analysis was justified, as with any new proposal of this sort.

RFC 1319 is an Informational memo that is now Historic, and RFC 6149 obsoletes it. That status, from the registry metadata, marks MD2 as no longer the specification to follow for new work.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1992 the authors considered MD2 strong enough for high-security signature systems, while noting that any new algorithm deserves more analysis. The RFC is now Historic, replaced by RFC 6149.

items.label: Append padding
items.desc: Extend the message to a multiple of 16 bytes with 1 to 16 padding bytes.

items.label: Append checksum
items.desc: Add a 16-byte checksum computed through the 256-byte pi-derived permutation table.

items.label: Initialize buffer
items.desc: Set a 48-byte working buffer to zero.

items.label: Process blocks
items.desc: Mix each 16-byte block into the buffer in 18 rounds of byte substitutions.

items.label: Output
items.desc: The first 16 bytes of the buffer are the message digest.
